comparison: Perfect agreement on claims C1-C4 regarding qPCR assay validation. Both evaluations rate as SUPPORTED with high praise for methodological rigor. OpenEval emphasizes technical metrics (LOD/LOQ, CV<2%), while peer reviewers highlight 'state-of-the-art methods' and 'robust and sensitive qPCR method.'

Perfect agreement on claims C5-C6 regarding oocyst quantification validation. Both rate as SUPPORTED. OpenEval provides statistical details (OR=14.68, p<0.0001, N=457), while peer reviewers accept methods without specific critique, noting the study 'establish[es] clear positive correlations.'

Perfect agreement on claims C7-C13 regarding EIP and infection burden relationship. Both rate as SUPPORTED. OpenEval details dose-response statistics (mixed-effects logistic regression, N=266), while peer reviewers explicitly affirm 'higher sporozoite loads are associated with earlier colonization' as a key finding.

Perfect agreement on claims C14-C16 regarding oocyst maturation dynamics. Both rate as SUPPORTED. OpenEval notes cautious interpretation due to modest sample sizes (N=12, N=19), while peer reviewers accept as part of 'very high-quality data that was well-analyzed.'

Strong agreement on claims C17-C22 regarding oocyst rupture correlation with salivary gland load. Both rate as SUPPORTED. OpenEval provides detailed statistics (ρ=0.80, p<0.0001, N=1,854 oocysts), peer reviewers accept as key finding. Peer review also includes C66 and C104 (main conclusions), showing broader grouping of related claims.

Perfect agreement on claims C23-C24 regarding artificial skin assay validation. Both rate as SUPPORTED with high praise. OpenEval emphasizes technical validation (no signal in unexposed areas), while peer reviewers highlight 'innovative experimental setup' and 'state-of-the-art artificial skin assay.'

Agreement on claims C25-C27, C30 regarding expelling prevalence and lack of association with infection intensity. Both rate as SUPPORTED. OpenEval notes proper reporting of non-significant result (p=0.1880), peer reviewers state 'no clear association...suggesting most infections reach sufficient threshold.' Peer review also includes C85 (non-expelling rate).

Significant disagreement on claims C29, C34-C36 regarding correlation between salivary gland load and expelled sporozoites. OpenEval rates as SUPPORTED with detailed statistics (ρ=0.35, N=112), while peer reviewers rate as UNCERTAIN, requesting additional analysis excluding high-infection mosquitoes and emphasizing need for 95% CI. Peer review groups with C31-C33, C37-C40 (broader set of expelling claims).

Disagreement on claims C37-C40 regarding low-infected mosquitoes expelling sporozoites. OpenEval rates as SUPPORTED (N=53 low-infected mosquitoes), while peer reviewers rate as UNCERTAIN, concerned that findings may not apply to natural settings where 'most mosquitoes have less than 5 oocysts.'

Related to claim C29 regarding median expelled sporozoites. OpenEval includes C29 in R8 (SUPPORTED), while peer reviewers address it separately in R9 (UNCERTAIN), requesting analysis at different infection intensity ranges to ensure relevance to natural settings.

Strong agreement on claims C41-C47 regarding field study design and infection outcomes. Both rate as SUPPORTED with high praise for including field validation. OpenEval notes technical limitations (discordant results), peer reviewers emphasize that 'both combinations showed statistically significant correlations' strengthening validity. Peer review also includes C48-C50 (oocyst rupture in field samples).

Agreement on claims C48-C50 regarding oocyst rupture rates in field samples. Both rate as SUPPORTED. OpenEval provides detailed statistics (87.8% rupture rate, N=421 oocysts), peer reviewers accept as part of field validation showing 'consistent results further strengthening quality.'

Strong agreement on claims C51-C55 regarding field expelling data. Both rate as SUPPORTED. OpenEval details higher expelling prevalence (89% vs 53%) and larger inoculum (1,035 vs 136) in field vs lab, peer reviewers accept as 'well-analyzed and presented' with 'consistent results.' Peer review also includes C60 (non-blood-feeding expelling).

Perfect agreement on claims C56-C58 regarding multiclonal infections in field samples. Both rate as SUPPORTED. OpenEval notes modest but adequate sample size (N=22), peer reviewers accept without critique as supporting broader field validation quality.

Agreement on claims C59-C60 regarding non-blood-feeding mosquitoes expelling sporozoites. Both rate as SUPPORTED. OpenEval cites consistency with rodent malaria studies (N=53 mosquitoes), peer reviewers accept as part of field data validation.

Disagreement on claims C61-C63 regarding oocyst rupture correlation in field data. OpenEval rates as SUPPORTED with strong statistics (ρ=0.80, N=25-30), while peer reviewers rate as UNCERTAIN, concerned about generalizability due to infection levels 'rarely observed in wild-caught mosquitoes' potentially causing 'overestimation.'

Disagreement on claims C64-C65 regarding stronger correlation in natural vs cultured infections. OpenEval rates as SUPPORTED (ρ=0.71 vs 0.35), while peer reviewers rate as UNCERTAIN with same concerns about high infection levels dominating results and overestimating importance under natural conditions.

Disagreement on claims C88-C90 regarding differences between experimental settings. OpenEval rates as SUPPORTED, noting ~14-fold difference in expelled sporozoites, while peer reviewers rate as UNCERTAIN, questioning whether correlations dominated by rarely-observed high infection levels apply to natural transmission.

Agreement on main conclusions C66-C68, C104-C106 regarding ~95% oocyst rupture and associations between infection burden, EIP, and inoculum. OpenEval rates as SUPPORTED based on collective evidence, peer reviewers also rate as SUPPORTED, stating authors 'establish clear positive correlations.' Peer review groups with oocyst rupture data (C17-C22).

Partial disagreement on conclusions C67-C68, C105-C106 regarding implications for infectiousness. OpenEval rates as SUPPORTED, while peer reviewers rate as UNCERTAIN, noting 'whether all expelled sporozoites are equally infectious is unknown' and 'the central question...remains open,' suggesting associations don't definitively prove differential infectiousness.

Perfect agreement on claims C69-C73 regarding study significance and novelty. Both rate as SUPPORTED. OpenEval justifies 'first direct evidence for P. falciparum' claim, peer reviewers explicitly affirm this 'challenges the often-made assumption that all infected mosquitoes are equally infectious' and provides evidence against 'long-believed dogma.'

Agreement on claims C74-C76 regarding comparison with prior work. Both rate as SUPPORTED. OpenEval validates comparisons with Stone et al. 2013 and explanations for differences, peer reviewers accept contextual comparisons and praise methodological differences (individual mosquito analysis) as strengths.

Agreement on claims C77-C80 regarding sporozoite per oocyst estimates. Both rate as SUPPORTED. OpenEval contextualizes with historical literature (Pringle 1965, Wang et al. 2018), peer reviewers accept as part of high-quality data showing species differences from rodent models.

Agreement on claim C77 regarding proportion of sporozoites reaching salivary glands. Both rate as SUPPORTED. OpenEval notes appropriate citations, peer reviewers accept as part of contextual discussion without critique.

Agreement on claims C81-C84 regarding single-oocyst mosquitoes and species differences. Both rate as SUPPORTED. OpenEval emphasizes 92.9% of single-oocyst mosquitoes had >1,000 sporozoites (N=28), peer reviewers note 'important observation suggests low-density gametocyte carriers...could nevertheless contribute to malaria transmission.'

Agreement on claim C85 regarding 39% non-expelling rate. Both rate as SUPPORTED. OpenEval notes calculation from data, peer reviewers discuss as 'no clear association between salivary gland burdens and prevalence of expelling.'

Agreement on claims C86-C87 regarding mechanistic explanations for non-expelling. Both rate as SUPPORTED. OpenEval notes appropriate citations to prior work (Medica and Sinnis 2005), peer reviewers accept contextual comparisons without critique.

Agreement on claims C91-C92 regarding EIP findings and study design distinctions. Both rate as SUPPORTED. OpenEval validates citations to prior inconsistent findings, peer reviewers accept contextual discussion and praise individual mosquito analysis as methodological strength.

Disagreement on claim C93 regarding heavily infected mosquitoes being infectious sooner and more infectious. OpenEval rates as SUPPORTED based on combined evidence, while peer reviewers rate as UNCERTAIN, stating 'whether all expelled sporozoites are equally infectious is unknown' and this is 'not directly addressed in the study.'

Agreement on uncertainty for claims C94-C95 regarding submicroscopic carriers. OpenEval rates as UNCERTAIN, noting explicitly speculative nature ('conceivable,' 'would'), peer reviewers also rate as UNCERTAIN, with Reviewer 3 cautioning about applying findings from high infection levels to natural low-density infections.

Disagreement on claims C96-C98 regarding low oocyst burdens and transmission potential. OpenEval rates as SUPPORTED based on data from low-infected mosquitoes, while peer reviewers rate as UNCERTAIN with mixed views—Reviewer 2 supports contribution of low-density carriers, but Reviewer 3 questions applicability to natural settings.

Perfect agreement on claims C99-C103 regarding study limitations and future directions. Both rate as SUPPORTED. OpenEval notes appropriate identification of limitations and reasonable proposals for CHMI studies, peer reviewers implicitly support by noting 'whether all expelled sporozoites are equally infectious is unknown' and acknowledging need for additional studies.

Perfect agreement on claims C107-C111 regarding methodological details. Both rate as SUPPORTED with high praise. OpenEval notes standard protocols and appropriate citations, peer reviewers describe 'very rigorously designed studies using very well validated, state-of-the-art methods' with no concerns raised.
